summary: An excerpt from a fiction book (Book 10, part 39) set in a future economy of 3D printing and manufacturing. A narrator describes how a Chinese-led effort after the WTO catalogued nearly every 3D-printable plastic object, and how he prints parts from scavenged electronics and parts using an evolutionary algorithm. A conversation then turns to venture funding: a young man from a gigafund offers a $300,000 angel round, and an older, self-reliant businesswoman refuses it, arguing that the fund cannot deploy its capital efficiently at that scale.
one_line: Fiction excerpt about a 3D-printing designer and a venture-capital negotiation between a gigafund representative and a self-reliant businesswoman.
key_facts: After the WTO, the Chinese spent 25 years brute-forcing the problem-space of all possible 3D plastic objects that an American might pay money for.
The narrator said he can do fifty original designs in a day using an evolutionary algorithm.
The narrator said he uses more than 80 percent of any random container's payload, and the rest goes to feedstockers to be eaten by bacteria.
The narrator said that manufacturing is 'just monkey labor' and that every kid takes shop class nowadays, especially the girls.
The narrator made cars for his parents' anniversary, and he said no one wants to drive a truck anymore, preferring sub-micro solar cars.
The narrator says he could double his operation with 60 grand.
The gigafund representative's smallest angel round is 'Three hundred kay,' which is $300,000.
The gigafund representative proposed rolling her round up with five or six similar firms.
The narrator said that joining such a pool would increase communications and bureaucracy overhead by 3,000 percent.
The narrator said he is sixty years old and does not need to grow like a tumor anymore.
The narrator said he could turn 60 grand into 600 in six months.
The narrator said the gigafund's typical angel round is around a million, with Series A of ten or twenty and Series B of seventy.
The narrator told Mr Gonzales that the fund's smallest amount a franchisee can take is $300,000.
The narrator asked how the fund would spend a billion dollars in $300,000 increments, predicting it would be sitting on three quarters of that by the time the fund cashed out.
